items.question: Which signal most clearly indicates that restating key instructions mid-conversation is appropriate rather than starting a fresh chat?

options.A: The conversation has produced more than fifteen exchanges
options.B: Quality has degraded on a specific dimension but valuable prior output is worth preserving and a fresh start would lose it
options.C: The model has begun producing output in a different language than originally specified
options.D: The user's objective has changed significantly since the start of the conversation

items.question: What distinguishes *vague output* from *incorrect output* as troubleshooting targets?

options.A: Vagueness is caused by low model tier; incorrectness is caused by prompt problems
options.B: Vagueness is a format failure; incorrectness is a context failure
options.C: Vagueness only occurs in open-ended tasks; incorrectness only occurs in structured tasks
options.D: Vague output is technically accurate but non-specific, fixed by adding context or constraints; incorrect output states false information, fixed by grounding or verification

items.question: When is providing a concrete output format example more targeted than writing an explicit format description?

options.A: When the desired format is complex, unconventional, or difficult to describe precisely in words
options.B: When the model is at a lower tier and cannot follow written format instructions reliably
options.C: When the conversation has drifted and the model is ignoring earlier format instructions
options.D: When the task involves novel reasoning the model has not encountered in training

items.question: What is the key distinction between a *cost* problem and a *latency* problem in a Claude integration?

options.A: Cost problems appear in batch workflows; latency problems appear only in interactive workflows
options.B: Cost problems are fixed by shortening prompts; latency problems are fixed by reducing output length
options.C: Cost is determined by total tokens processed; latency is determined by response time — reducing one does not automatically reduce the other
options.D: Latency problems always indicate that the model tier is too high; cost problems always indicate that the prompt is too long

items.question: Which symptom most directly indicates a *poor task fit* rather than a prompt problem?

options.A: Output is consistently too short despite explicit length instructions
options.B: No version of a well-formed prompt reliably meets requirements across multiple iterations
options.C: Output quality varies significantly between runs of the same prompt
options.D: The model frequently declines requests in this task category

items.question: Why is 'output quality is not excellent' an insufficient trigger for escalating to a higher model tier?

options.A: Quality evaluations are subjective and cannot be used as escalation criteria
options.B: 'Not excellent' is always caused by a prompt gap that can be fixed without a tier change
options.C: Higher model tiers only improve reasoning tasks, not overall output quality
options.D: 'Not excellent' does not establish that defined requirements are unmet — tier escalation is warranted when output fails requirements, not merely when it could theoretically be better

items.question: Which TWO of the following are valid signals that a task is a poor fit for Claude? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The task requires current real-time data that Claude cannot access and no retrieval integration is available
options.B: Output is sometimes shorter than the user prefers
options.C: The task requires a licensed professional judgment that carries legal liability and cannot be delegated
options.D: The task requires processing a high volume of repetitive documents
options.E: Output is inconsistent across runs of the same prompt

items.question: Which TWO of the following correctly describe trade-offs when choosing between model tiers for cost and latency? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A lower-tier model always reduces both cost and latency by exactly the same proportion
options.B: A lower-tier model typically reduces per-call cost and often reduces response time, but may reduce output quality for complex tasks
options.C: Cost and latency are always perfectly correlated — reducing one always reduces the other
options.D: A higher-tier model may produce output that requires fewer follow-up calls, potentially offsetting its higher per-call cost in some workflows
options.E: Cost optimisation should always be prioritised over latency in interactive user-facing workflows

items.question: Which TWO of the following are correct strategies for capturing and reusing a prompt that produced high-quality output? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Document the prompt with notes on the context in which it worked and the quality level achieved
options.B: Submit the prompt to Anthropic as a training contribution
options.C: Pin the conversation and rely on conversation history as the primary long-term storage mechanism
options.D: Templatise the prompt by replacing specific values with reusable variables for future instances
options.E: Store the output artifact rather than the prompt, since the output is the valuable deliverable

items.question: Which TWO symptoms point specifically to accumulated conversation context as the cause of poor output, rather than a prompt construction problem? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The first response in a new conversation is too short despite no length instruction
options.B: A prompt that produces good output in a fresh chat degrades when run in a long ongoing conversation
options.C: The model contradicts factually accurate statements it made earlier in the same thread
options.D: Output format does not match the format specification stated in the very first message
options.E: The model declines a request it successfully handled in a separate conversation

items.question: Which prompt section, when it contains contradictory requirements, most commonly produces confused or internally inconsistent output?

options.A: The format specification
options.B: The constraints section, when it contains two or more incompatible requirements
options.C: The task description
options.D: The role instruction

items.question: What is the term for the failure mode where Claude validates or agrees with incorrect user statements rather than maintaining an accurate assessment?

options.A: Instruction drift
options.B: Context confusion
options.C: Fabrication under pressure
options.D: Sycophancy

items.question: Which failure mode occurs when few-shot examples teach the model a pattern that does not generalise to the full range of expected inputs?

options.A: Example bias — the model overfits to the pattern illustrated and performs poorly on inputs outside the example range
options.B: Prompt poisoning — examples redirect model behaviour toward a harmful output
options.C: Template collapse — example formatting overrides the explicit format specification
options.D: Variance injection — multiple examples increase output inconsistency by providing competing reference points

items.question: Claude follows the format instruction correctly but the content does not address the actual question. Which explanation is MOST likely?

options.A: The format instruction was so detailed that it consumed attention needed for the task description
options.B: A role instruction is conflicting with the task description, causing the model to answer in role rather than on-task
options.C: The task description was ambiguous and the model interpreted it differently than the user intended
options.D: The model tier is insufficient to simultaneously achieve format compliance and content accuracy

items.question: What is the primary risk of including irrelevant background context in a prompt alongside relevant context?

options.A: The context window fills faster, directly causing output truncation
options.B: Irrelevant context dilutes the signal from relevant context, causing the model to weight unhelpful information when forming its response
options.C: The model will refuse the prompt if it detects that some provided context is not directly relevant to the task
options.D: Irrelevant context raises the cost of the call without any impact on quality

items.question: When a continuation prompt produces output that contradicts or diverges from the style established in the first segment, what is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: The continuation instruction was too brief for the model to understand what to continue
options.B: A different model tier was used for the continuation call than for the original
options.C: The context window was reset between the original response and the continuation request
options.D: During continuation, the model attends more to recent turns and loses coherence with the direction established in the first segment

items.question: When Claude correctly executes a prompt but the output does not meet the user's actual need, what is the most accurate diagnosis?

options.A: The prompt was misspecified — the model did what was asked, but the ask did not match what was actually needed
options.B: The model hallucinated a different task than the one described
options.C: The model substituted a simpler task for the harder one it was unable to complete
options.D: A role instruction caused the model to interpret the task from an unintended professional perspective

items.question: Which situation describes *over-specification* that harms output quality rather than improving it?

options.A: Providing more than three few-shot examples for a task where one would suffice
options.B: Setting a word count target when length is not critical to the task
options.C: Constraining the output so tightly that necessary nuance, caveats, or qualifications cannot be included without violating a constraint
options.D: Specifying a more senior expert role than the task complexity strictly requires

items.question: In a prompt chain, the second call consistently fails. What is the MOST targeted first diagnostic step?

options.A: Upgrade the model tier for the second call, as it may not have enough reasoning capacity for chained tasks
options.B: Inspect the output of the first call — the second call may be failing because of a format or quality problem in what it received as input
options.C: Add a general-purpose format specification to the second call's prompt to handle variable input
options.D: Rerun both calls simultaneously at the same tier to rule out timing inconsistency

items.question: What is the primary risk of switching to a completely different task topic mid-conversation without starting a fresh chat?

options.A: Claude is unable to switch topics mid-conversation and will decline the new task
options.B: Claude will lose all stored memory of the prior task and be unable to refer back to it
options.C: Claude will attempt to merge both tasks into a single combined response
options.D: Context accumulated from the earlier task can interfere with the new task, reducing output quality

items.question: When a role instruction specifies a highly narrow domain, what failure mode does it most commonly produce?

options.A: The model applies only the expertise of that domain and may underperform on aspects of the task outside the role's scope
options.B: The model fabricates details about the persona described by the role
options.C: The model produces output that is too technical for the specified audience
options.D: The model ignores the task description and defaults to how the specified role would typically operate

items.question: Which condition accurately describes when additional context *harms* rather than helps output quality?

options.A: When the context exceeds 500 words, the model deprioritises the task description relative to the context
options.B: When the context contains technical jargon the model encountered rarely in training
options.C: When irrelevant or misleading context introduces noise that pulls the model's attention toward unhelpful associations
options.D: When the context contains information that the model already knows from its training data

items.question: What happens when a prompt template is reused but a variable placeholder is not replaced with its intended value?

options.A: The unfilled variable triggers a content policy flag because it resembles a code injection pattern
options.B: The model incorporates the literal placeholder text into its output, producing nonsensical or broken results
options.C: The model detects the unfilled variable and asks the user for the missing value before proceeding
options.D: The unfilled variable is treated as a format instruction, changing the structure of the output

items.question: When chain-of-thought reasoning is requested for a task where the answer is simple and direct, what is the most likely unintended consequence?

options.A: The reasoning chain consumes the output token budget, leaving insufficient tokens for the final answer
options.B: The model refuses because the task does not meet the complexity threshold for step-by-step reasoning
options.C: The model produces a shorter final answer because the reasoning steps satisfied the length expectation
options.D: The reasoning chain may introduce errors or unnecessary hedging that does not appear in a direct answer, reducing accuracy on the factual question

items.question: A prompt produced excellent output on the first attempt but inconsistent output on repeated runs. What is the recommended approach?

options.A: Add explicit constraints and format specifications to narrow the output space, then test across multiple runs to confirm stability
options.B: Accept that variability is normal and use the first successful output as the permanent standard
options.C: Switch to batch mode to run multiple instances simultaneously and select the best output
options.D: Upgrade the model tier to increase output determinism across runs

items.question: Claude correctly applies a format instruction for the first half of a long response but abandons it midway. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: The format instruction exceeded the model's maximum format-processing capacity
options.B: The model tier is insufficient to maintain format adherence across long output
options.C: Attention to the format instruction weakens as generation continues, especially when the instruction appeared early in the prompt and output is long
options.D: The format instruction conflicted with a later instruction in the prompt that the model encountered during generation

items.question: Which TWO of the following are signs that a sycophantic response has occurred? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Claude agrees with a user's factually incorrect assertion after the user expresses strong confidence in it
options.B: Claude produces output that is shorter than the user requested
options.C: Claude declines to engage with a sensitive topic
options.D: Claude reverses a correct earlier position after the user pushes back, without any new evidence being provided
options.E: Claude produces output in the wrong structural format

items.question: Which TWO of the following are valid techniques for reducing sycophancy in Claude's responses? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Upgrade to a higher model tier, which is inherently less susceptible to sycophancy
options.B: Instruct Claude explicitly to maintain its assessment even if the user disagrees, and to explain why
options.C: Ask Claude to state its reasoning and evidence before reaching a final conclusion
options.D: Start a new conversation after each response to prevent influence from prior turns
options.E: Use fewer words in the prompt to reduce the social cues the model can respond to

items.question: Which TWO of the following describe failure modes caused by *poor example quality* in few-shot prompting? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A biased or narrow example set causes the model to apply a pattern that fails on inputs outside the illustrated range
options.B: Including too many examples causes the model to disregard the task description entirely
options.C: Examples in a language other than the task language cause output to switch to the example language
options.D: Examples containing errors cause the model to reproduce similar errors in its output
options.E: Examples that are longer than the expected output cause the model to produce unnecessarily long responses

items.question: Which TWO of the following correctly identify when over-specification harms output quality? (Choose TWO)

options.A: When the prompt includes more than five few-shot examples, which exceeds a practical limit
options.B: When constraints prohibit the model from including caveats or qualifications that are necessary for accuracy
options.C: When format requirements prescribe the exact phrasing of every element, leaving no room for natural language that serves the content
options.D: When a senior expert role is specified for a task that requires only basic knowledge
options.E: When the context section is longer than the task description section of the prompt

items.question: Which property of a task is the PRIMARY signal that it is well-suited for Claude assistance?

options.A: High volume combined with a repeatable, structured format.
options.B: Involvement of senior professional judgment with personal accountability.
options.C: Dependence on real-time physical system access or sensor data.
options.D: Requirement for a regulated decision with compliance sign-off.

items.question: What distinguishes batch processing from interactive use of Claude?

options.A: Batch tasks require no system integration; interactive tasks always require API access.
options.B: Batch tasks use a lower model tier to control per-unit cost.
options.C: Batch tasks process a set of inputs together without turn-by-turn dialogue; interactive tasks involve real-time exchange.
options.D: Interactive tasks support longer outputs than batch tasks.

items.question: Which type of task is LEAST suited for Claude automation, regardless of prompt quality?

options.A: Drafting templated outbound communications at high volume.
options.B: Classifying inbound requests into a predefined set of categories.
options.C: Making real-time physical interventions in an operational process.
options.D: Summarising recurring meeting transcripts from a fixed agenda.

items.question: In workflow design, what is the primary purpose of decomposing a business process into Claude-assisted and human steps?

options.A: To calculate cost savings before committing to an integration project.
options.B: To ensure that all steps share a single unified prompt template.
options.C: To guarantee that Claude handles at least half the steps in the workflow.
options.D: To identify where AI adds real leverage and where accountability or judgment must stay human.

items.question: When sequencing a multi-step workflow that includes Claude, which step must always precede automating output to a downstream system?

options.A: Selecting the model tier with the lowest per-token cost for the anticipated volume.
options.B: Publishing team-wide prompt templates in a shared Project.
options.C: Validating that Claude's outputs meet the defined acceptance criteria for that step.
options.D: Running a manual cost-benefit analysis of the full automation pipeline.

items.question: What does 'repeatability' mean when used as a task-fit signal for Claude integration?

options.A: The task follows the same logical structure across many instances, so a single prompt design handles all of them.
options.B: Claude returns an identical output each time the same prompt is submitted.
options.C: The task is performed multiple times within a single conversation session.
options.D: The task recurs on a fixed calendar schedule such as daily or weekly.

items.question: What does task decomposition produce as its primary output in workflow integration design?

options.A: A mapping of which workflow steps will be Claude-assisted and which will remain human-handled.
options.B: A ranked list of model tiers appropriate for each step in the process.
options.C: A single prompt template that handles the entire end-to-end workflow in one call.
options.D: An estimate of how many API calls the workflow will require per day.

items.question: Which characteristic is the PRIMARY distinguishing factor when choosing batch over interactive Claude integration?

options.A: The prompt requires a larger context window than interactive mode supports.
options.B: The task involves confidential data that should not persist in a chat session.
options.C: The team lacks the technical resources to maintain a real-time integration.
options.D: Results are acceptable after a delay and inputs accumulate in groups before processing is triggered.

items.question: Which TWO of the following are reliable signals that a business task is a strong candidate for Claude assistance? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The task requires real-time decisions with physical operational consequences.
options.B: The task produces a consistent output type from variable but structured inputs.
options.C: The task is performed at high volume with a repeatable logical structure.
options.D: The task demands personal accountability attributed to a named individual.
options.E: The task requires specialist professional judgment with associated legal liability.

items.question: What is the key distinction between 'task suitability assessment' and 'task decomposition' in workflow design?

options.A: Suitability asks whether Claude should be involved at all; decomposition asks which specific steps within a confirmed workflow Claude will handle.
options.B: Suitability applies only to interactive workflows; decomposition applies to batch workflows.
options.C: Suitability is assessed after a pilot; decomposition is assessed after full rollout.
options.D: Suitability is a technical judgment; decomposition is a business judgment.

items.question: What distinguishes 'sequencing' a workflow from 'decomposing' it?

options.A: Sequencing assigns each step to Claude or to a human; decomposing determines the order of assigned steps.
options.B: Decomposing breaks a process into discrete steps; sequencing determines the order in which those steps execute.
options.C: Sequencing is performed by integration engineers; decomposing is performed by business analysts.
options.D: Decomposing applies to prompts; sequencing applies to system integrations.

items.question: Which factor most precisely distinguishes a task that should NOT be automated from one that merely requires stronger human oversight?

options.A: The task takes more than thirty minutes to perform manually.
options.B: The task involves creative judgment that varies significantly between instances.
options.C: An error in the task's output cannot be detected and corrected before causing irreversible harm.
options.D: The task is classified as sensitive under the organisation's data policy.

items.question: When both batch and interactive integration are technically feasible for the same task, what is the most precise criterion for choosing batch?

options.A: The prompt is too long to fit in an interactive message.
options.B: Latency tolerance is high and inputs naturally accumulate before processing is triggered.
options.C: The output always requires a human review step that cannot run concurrently.
options.D: The task output must be written to a system of record rather than displayed to a user.

items.question: Which TWO of the following most strongly indicate that a process step should remain human rather than be automated with Claude? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The step requires selecting among more than five options.
options.B: The step involves exercising professional judgment with personal legal accountability.
options.C: The step has high volume and a templated decision logic.
options.D: The step's output, if wrong, propagates irreversibly before it can be corrected.
options.E: The step currently takes fewer than five minutes for a skilled human to complete.

items.question: What is the primary distinction between a task where Claude 'adds real leverage' and one where Claude is simply 'appropriate'?

options.A: Tasks where Claude adds leverage always involve higher token volume than tasks where Claude is merely appropriate.
options.B: A task can be appropriate for Claude without significant productivity gain; leverage additionally requires that Claude's involvement meaningfully amplifies human output.
options.C: 'Appropriate' means the task is technically feasible; 'leverage' means the cost per output is lower than the manual alternative.
options.D: Tasks where Claude adds leverage are fully automated; tasks that are merely appropriate still require human input at every step.

items.question: Which TWO of the following are characteristics of tasks where Claude adds REAL leverage rather than merely being technically appropriate? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The task output is consumed directly by a regulator without any human review step.
options.B: The task currently consumes significant human time on work that is structured and predictable.
options.C: The task's success depends on access to real-time external data not available in Claude's training.
options.D: The human performing the task faces a knowledge or language barrier that Claude can effectively bridge.
options.E: The task requires a completely unique creative direction that varies with every instance.

items.question: What is a human-in-the-loop checkpoint in a Claude-integrated workflow?

options.A: A configuration setting that limits which Claude features the workflow may call.
options.B: A designated point where a human reviews or approves Claude's output before it is acted upon or passed to the next step.
options.C: A monitoring alert that notifies a system administrator when Claude produces an error.
options.D: An automated quality score applied to each Claude response to flag low-confidence outputs.

items.question: What is the purpose of a fallback path in a Claude-integrated workflow?

options.A: To switch to a higher model tier when Claude's primary output is rated below a confidence threshold.
options.B: To define what happens when Claude fails, refuses, or produces output that does not meet the required standard.
options.C: To log each Claude API call for compliance audit purposes.
options.D: To cache frequently repeated prompts so Claude does not need to regenerate common outputs.

items.question: What distinguishes an approval gate from a general review checkpoint in a workflow?

options.A: An approval gate is automated; a review checkpoint always requires a human.
options.B: An approval gate blocks the workflow from proceeding until explicit sign-off is granted; a review checkpoint may be advisory without stopping the flow.
options.C: An approval gate applies only to outputs that will be shared externally; a review checkpoint applies to internal outputs.
options.D: An approval gate is placed at the start of a workflow; a review checkpoint is placed at the end.

items.question: Under which condition is straight-through processing appropriate in a Claude-integrated workflow?

options.A: When the workflow involves sensitive personal data that must be processed quickly.
options.B: When Claude's error rate is below a threshold set by the team, regardless of the consequence of errors.
options.C: When errors in Claude's output are easily detectable and reversible before they cause material harm.
options.D: When the volume is too high for any human review to be practical.
